messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 42
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: African
  relationship_status: Divorced
  occupation: Factory Worker
  trauma_type: Torture
  pcl5: 73

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Proximity: Physical proximity, Name Reminders: Hearing related names, Weather Similarity: Similar weather conditions to when the event happened
  Maladaptive Strategies: Heavy Makeup: heavy make-up, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time, Avoid Similar Clothes: avoid wearing similar clothes
  Threat: Intrusion Monitoring: I listen for sounds that might mean someone is entering my home, Body Reacts Before Mind: My body reacts to danger before I have even had time to think, Startle to Sounds: I jump or startle at ordinary sounds that would not bother most people
  Memory: Story Feels Unreal: The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me, Olfactory Recall: When I think about the frightening event I can sometimes smell things that I smelt when the frightening event happened., Memory Feels Alien: The memory feels like it belongs to someone else rather than to me
  Negative Appraisals: World is Dangerous: The world is a dangerous place, No Longer Capable: I am no longer capable of doing the things that defined me, Body Unreliable: I can no longer trust my own body

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Amara

Amara was thirty-four when armed men entered the compound where she worked as a nurse in a rural clinic in South Sudan. That was eight years ago. She had been checking supplies in the back room when the shooting started—a sound she would come to know in her body before her mind could name it. The men separated the staff. What happened over the next hours existed in her memory as something both vivid and impossible, a sequence of violence and humiliation so extreme that even now, sitting in the therapist's office, she could not quite believe it had occurred to her. Sometimes she wondered if the memory belonged to someone else entirely, a story she had absorbed rather than lived. Yet her body knew. Her body remembered with perfect, treacherous clarity.

When she finally escaped the country two years later, she carried that memory like a second skeleton. She had moved to the United States, found work at a factory assembling medical components—ironic, she thought sometimes, that she was back around medical equipment but in a different form of captivity. The factory floor was loud and predictable. She could control it. What she could not control was the world outside.

The first year in America, Amara had tried to live normally. She wore her old clothes, the bright fabrics she loved. But in the spring, when the weather turned warm and humid, matching the season when she had been taken, her body had begun to betray her. The smell of rain on hot earth—a smell that had been present that day—would arrive on the breeze, and suddenly she could not breathe. She had stopped wearing the clothes associated with that time. She had stopped going outside when the weather felt similar. Gradually, she had narrowed the world.

At home, she listened. Always listening. For footsteps on the stairs, for the sound of a key in the lock, for voices that might indicate someone was coming. Her apartment was on the second floor, and she had memorized every creak of the building, every sound that meant safety and every sound that meant danger. When her ex-husband had tried to visit last year—a man named Kofi, a name that appeared sometimes in conversation—she had felt her entire body tense, flooded with a fear that made no logical sense. He was not one of them. But her body did not distinguish. Her body reacted to danger before her mind could catch up, before she could remind herself that she was safe, that this was America, that it was only a name.

She had taken to wearing heavy makeup, layers of it, as though she could paint over what had happened to her skin, make herself unrecognizable even to herself. At the factory, her supervisor had asked if she was all right. She had said yes. She had not mentioned that she flinched at every unexpected sound, that her coworkers had begun to notice how she startled at the normal noises of the production line—the pneumatic hiss of machinery, the clang of metal on metal. She had not mentioned that she had stopped attending the evening shifts because darkness made the listening worse, and she had been quietly demoted to day work, a consequence no one discussed but everyone understood.

What frightened Amara most was that her body no longer felt like her own. She could not trust it to react appropriately, to distinguish between real danger and the ghosts of danger. She was no longer capable of the things that had once defined her—the steadiness, the presence of mind, the ability to help others without falling apart. The world had shown itself to be a place where men could take what they wanted, and no amount of vigilance could prevent that. She was forty-two now, and she had come to believe that she would spend the rest of her life listening for footsteps, jumping at sounds, trying to paint over the past with makeup and mental distraction. Last month, her sister had finally convinced her to call someone. She had made the appointment. She was here. And what she was most afraid of, more than anything, was that this was simply who she was now.
